paras: The Pine Street attack on George Graham's home was an assault by a crowd of white men on the house of a newly arrived Black tenant near 25th and Pine streets in Philadelphia in late April 1919. Black residents met the attackers with gunfire, and between three and nine white men were wounded before police ended the fight. Black newspapers across the country reported it as a white attack on a Black home that the residents had beaten back.

Graham and his family had moved into the Pine street house a few days, or about a week, before the attack. According to the Chicago Defender, the white neighbors objected to his living there. The Philadelphia Tribune set the episode beside the attacks on Black homebuyers of the year before and complained that white real-estate dealers charged Black buyers four or five hundred dollars more than whites.

Shortly after midnight on a Saturday night, a crowd the Tribune put at "30 or more" attacked the house, smashing its windows and battering in the door. The Afro-American and the Defender counted 75 whites against about 40 Black people, and said the whites came with bricks and tried to eject Graham. Black men from the house and nearby homes came out with firearms, clubs and bricks, and the two sides fought in the street.

A riot call brought police from the 19th district, who broke up the crowd after what the Afro-American called a fifteen-minute battle. The Tribune and the Defender reported three white men shot, the Afro-American said Black residents "shot three, wounded four", and the Associated Negro Press reported nine white men seriously wounded. No deaths were reported.

According to the Tribune, the three wounded white youths were treated at Polyclinic Hospital and then held on a riot charge for a further hearing. Graham and other occupants of the house were also locked up; the Defender said Graham was held under $400 bail while ten others were discharged for lack of evidence. Graham was released at the hearing. No report of a trial of the white youths appears in the coverage.

Only Black papers carried the episode in the coverage examined, beginning with a brief in the Baltimore Afro-American of 2 May under a "Riots in Philadelphia" heading. The Philadelphia Tribune of 3 May folded its account into a front-page commentary that criticized the arrest of Black defenders and praised Graham for learning "home defense and self defense." The Chicago Defender headlined its report "Stop Whites with Guns in Philadelphia Riot."

The Associated Negro Press dispatch described the attackers as "a gang that has long terrorized residents" and Graham as a man who had "always lived uprightly in the community." It ran on 10 May in the Cleveland Advocate as "Whites Resent Intrusion of Race; Fight Follows," in the Kansas City Sun, and in the Omaha Monitor as "Wound White Rowdies Who Terrorize Residents." Later printings followed in the St. Louis Argus on 16 May, under "Nine Whites Wounded in Assault on Negro Residents in Phila," and the Metropolis Weekly Gazette on 23 May, while a few of its sentences surfaced inside an unrelated editorial in the Phoenix Tribune of 17 May.

The count of wounded whites differs: the local Tribune, which named the hospital and the youths held, and the Defender give three, while the wire gives nine. The house number is 2535 Pine in the Afro-American and the wire but 2533 in the Defender. The wire's "this morning" under datelines of 6 to 9 May conflicts with the earlier reports printed on 2 and 3 May, which place the attack on a Sunday morning in late April.

reader.title: Pine Street attack on George Graham's home (Philadelphia, 1919)
bases: A white crowd attacked the house of a newly arrived Black tenant, smashing its windows and door and trying to eject the family, and a street fight with Black residents followed (A2, A3, A4).

The local Philadelphia Tribune, the Afro-American's brief, the Chicago Defender and the Associated Negro Press wire independently agree that whites attacked Graham's newly occupied Pine street house and were met with gunfire (A2, A3, A4, A6).

accounts.label: Local Black weekly (Philadelphia Tribune)
accounts.gist: A crowd of 30 or more attacked Graham's house after midnight Saturday; whites and Black people fought until 19th district police arrived; three white youths shot were treated at Polyclinic Hospital and held on a riot charge, while Graham and other occupants were locked up and released.

accounts.label: Afro-American brief
accounts.gist: Datelined 28 April: 75 whites tried to push back 40 Negroes and eject Graham from 2535 Pine; the whites charged with bricks, and Black residents shot three and wounded four before police reserves stopped the fifteen-minute battle.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender correspondent
accounts.gist: Three white men shot during a riot at 25th and Pine after white neighbors attacked the 2533 Pine house; Graham was held under $400 bail and released at the hearing.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press wire
accounts.gist: Fighting between newly arrived Black tenants and 'a gang that has long terrorized residents' left nine white men seriously wounded; it began when a mob broke open the door at 2535 Pine and tried to eject Graham's family.

framing.detail: The Philadelphia Tribune set the attack in a front-page piece headed with a garbled 'Shoot to Kill' slogan, compared it to the 1918 house attacks, criticized the arrest of Black defenders and white dealers who charged Black buyers more, and endorsed 'home defense and self defense'.
The Defender headlined 'Stop Whites with Guns in Philadelphia Riot' and said white neighbors objected to Graham living there.

The ANP wire called the attackers 'a gang that has long terrorized residents' and Graham a man who 'has always lived uprightly'; papers ran it as 'Whites Resent Intrusion of Race', 'Riot in Philadelphi' and 'Nine Whites Wounded in Assault on Negro Residents'.

conflicts.note: The local Tribune, which names the hospital and the youths held, and the Defender both say three; the nine of the ANP wire is the outlier.
